units.title: Hangul
units.subtitle: Read Korean in six short lessons

steps.text: 안녕! I'm Gochi. Korean letters are called Hangul, and you can learn to read them in a few lessons.
Letters stack into blocks. Each block is one syllable.
A vowel can't stand alone, so it sits next to ㅇ. Here, ㅇ is silent.

steps.why: 아 has the short line pointing right.
In 우 the line points down. In 오 it points up.
오 is 'o' and 이 is 'i'.

steps.text: Now consonants. Each one goes before the vowel in the block.

steps.translation: ga (ㄱ is between g and k)
da (ㄷ is between d and t)
ra (ㄹ is a light r, close to l)
ba (ㅂ is between b and p)

steps.text: Put them together and you can read real words.

steps.why: 바 + 다 = 바다.
ㄱ is g, ㅅ is s.
ㅁ is a little box, like closed lips.

steps.text: Add one more short line to a vowel and it gets a 'y' sound.
ㅐ and ㅔ sound almost the same today, like the 'e' in bed.
Some vowels join together. ㅗ + ㅏ = ㅘ (wa), ㅜ + ㅓ = ㅝ (wo).

steps.why: 요 is 오 with one more line.
네 means yes. 개 is dog.
ㄱ + ㅘ makes 과 (gwa).

steps.text: Some consonants come with a puff of air. Hold your hand in front of your mouth and feel it.
Double letters are tense: short, tight, no air.
Which one has a puff of air?
steps.why: ㅋ has an extra line and a puff of air. ㄲ is tight with no air.
아빠 is dad. Mom is 엄마.

steps.text: How do you read 차 (car, tea)?
steps.why: ㅊ is ㅈ with a puff of air: cha.

steps.text: A consonant can also sit at the bottom of a block. It's called 받침.
Bottom letters only make 7 sounds: k, n, t, l, m, p, ng.
At the bottom, ㅅ, ㅈ and ㅊ all sound like t. ㅇ at the bottom says ng.
What sound does ㅇ make at the bottom of 강?
steps.why: ㅇ is silent at the top but says ng at the bottom.
물 is water. 밥 is rice.
ㅅ at the bottom sounds like t.

steps.text: Last trick: when a bottom letter meets a silent ㅇ, it slides over to the next block.
Now you can read real Korean. Try these.

steps.why: ㄱ slides into the silent ㅇ: 한구거.
감사합니다 is a polite thank you.
서 + 울 = 서울.

steps.text: 잘했어요! You can read Hangul now. Next, you'll introduce yourself in Korean.
Let's learn words to talk about yourself. Tap each one to hear it.
Add 사람 (person) after a country to say where someone is from.

steps.why: 일본 (Japan) + 사람 (person).
회사 is company, so 회사원 is a company worker.
선생님 is teacher. 학생 is student.

steps.text: To say 'I am a ___' or 'it is ___', add 이에요 or 예요 to the noun.
If the noun ends in a consonant, add 이에요.
If it ends in a vowel, add 예요.
For a question, use the same words and raise your voice at the end.

steps.why: 회사원 ends in ㄴ, a consonant, so 이에요.
의사 ends in a vowel, so 예요.
사람 ends in ㅁ, so 이에요.

steps.text: 은/는 marks what you're talking about, like 'as for...'.
After a consonant use 은. After a vowel use 는.
씨 goes after a name to be polite. Never use it with your own name.

steps.why: 저 ends in a vowel, so 는.
이름 ends in ㅁ, so 은.
Use 씨 for other people, not yourself.

lessons.title: Put it together: nice to meet you

steps.text: Here's how a first meeting sounds. Listen to each line.

steps.translation: Yes, I'm a student. And you, Minsu?

steps.text: Adding 요 to a name, like 민수 씨는요?, means 'and you?'.

steps.why: You say it when you meet someone for the first time.

steps.text: How do you say 'And you, Hana?'
steps.why: Name + 씨는요? means 'and you?'.

steps.text: 잘했어요! Now you can introduce yourself in Korean.
Let's meet the family. Tap each word to hear it.
Older siblings depend on who is speaking.
A man talks about his older sister. Which word?
steps.why: Men say 누나. Women say 언니.
동생 is any younger brother or sister.
할머니 is grandmother. 할아버지 is grandfather.

steps.text: 이/가 marks who or what does something, or new information.
After a consonant use 이. After a vowel use 가.

steps.translation: My younger sibling is a student.

steps.text: When you ask 'who?', the answer uses 이/가.

steps.why: 형 ends in ㅇ, so 이.
누나 ends in a vowel, so 가.
To answer 'who?', use 이/가.

steps.text: To say 'is not', use 이/가 아니에요.

steps.translation: My older brother isn't a doctor.

steps.text: Same rule: 이 after a consonant, 가 after a vowel.
Answer yes with 네 and no with 아니요.

steps.translation: No, I'm not a cook. I'm a nurse.

steps.why: 선생님 ends in ㅁ, so 이.
의사 ends in a vowel, so 가 아니에요.
아니요 is no, then 이/가 아니에요.

lessons.title: Put it together: a family photo

steps.text: Hana is showing Minsu a family photo. Listen.

steps.translation: No, she's not a student. She's a nurse.
Yes, that's my younger sibling. They're in high school.

steps.text: Koreans say 우리 (our) for family, even when it's 'my' in English.
How do you say 'my mom' naturally?
steps.why: Use 우리 for your own family.
누구 means who.

steps.translation: My younger sibling isn't a student.

steps.text: 잘했어요! You can introduce your family now.

units.title: Daily life
units.subtitle: Say what you like and do

steps.text: Korean verbs end in 다 in the dictionary. Let's learn some you'll use every day.

steps.why: 마시다 is to drink. 먹다 is to eat.
공부 means study, and 하다 means to do.
영화 is a movie. A TV series is 드라마.

steps.text: -습니다 is the formal polite style. You hear it in the news, at work, and in announcements.
Take off 다. If the stem ends in a consonant, add 습니다.
If it ends in a vowel, add ㅂ니다 to the last block.
For questions, use 습니까 or ㅂ니까. 이에요 becomes 입니다 in this style.

steps.why: 먹 ends in a consonant, so 습니다.
보 ends in a vowel, so ㅂ goes under it: 봅니다.
-ㅂ니까 makes a formal question.

steps.text: 을/를 marks what you eat, drink, watch or like.
After a consonant use 을. After a vowel use 를.
도 means 'too' or 'also'. It takes the place of 은/는, 이/가 or 을/를.

steps.why: 영화 ends in a vowel, so 를.
빵 ends in ㅇ, a consonant, so 을.
도 replaces 을/를. Don't use both.

lessons.title: Put it together: what do you like?

steps.text: Hana and Minsu are talking about what they like. Listen.

steps.translation: I like dramas too. I like movies too.

steps.text: 무엇 means 'what'. In speech it often shortens to 뭐.

steps.why: 무엇 is what, 좋아합니까 is 'do you like'.
차 ends in a vowel, so 를.

steps.text: 잘했어요! You can talk about what you like now.
Let's learn words for school. Tap each one to hear it.

steps.why: 도서관 is a library. 교실 is a classroom.
의자 is a chair. 책상 is a desk.
배우다 is to learn. 읽다 is to read.

steps.text: To join two nouns, use 과/와 or 하고. They mean 'and'.
과 after a consonant, 와 after a vowel. 하고 works after anything and sounds more casual.
하고 and 과/와 can also mean 'with'.

steps.why: 책상 ends in ㅇ, so 과.
의자 ends in a vowel, so 와.
하고 doesn't change. It's common in speech.

steps.text: 의 means 's or 'of'. It goes between the owner and the thing.
In speech, 의 often sounds like 에.
'My' is 제. It's short for 저의.

steps.why: Owner first, then 의, then the thing.

steps.text: What is the short form of 저의?
steps.why: 저의 becomes 제. 제 가방 means my bag.
제 친구 means my friend.

lessons.title: Put it together: in the classroom

steps.text: Hana finds a book in the classroom. Listen.

steps.translation: Minsu learns Korean with a friend.

steps.text: 아닙니다 is the formal form of 아니에요.
이것 means 'this thing'. You'll learn 이, 그, 저 later.
What does 제 책이 아닙니다 mean?
steps.why: 아닙니다 means 'is not', in the formal style.
가방 ends in ㅇ, so 과.

steps.translation: I read a book with a friend.

steps.text: 잘했어요! You can talk about school now.
Koreans talk about the weather a lot. Let's learn the words.

steps.why: 겨울 is winter. 여름 is summer.
춥다 is cold. 덥다 is hot.
눈 is snow. It also means eye.

steps.text: -아요/어요 is the polite style people use every day. It's softer than -습니다.
Look at the last vowel of the stem. If it's ㅏ or ㅗ, add 아요.
덥다 and 춥다 change shape: 더워요, 추워요. Just learn them as they are.

steps.why: The vowel in 작 is ㅏ, so 아요.
하다 becomes 해요.
The vowel in 읽 is ㅣ, so 어요.

steps.text: To say 'not', take off 다 and add 지 않아요.
No shape changes here: 춥다 becomes 춥지 않아요, not 추워지 않아요.

steps.why: Stem 크 + 지 않아요.
Stem 좋 + 지 않아요.
Stem 먹 + 지 않아요.

lessons.title: Put it together: how's the weather?

steps.translation: The weather isn't good. It's raining.
No, it's not cold. It's cool.
I like spring. Spring is warm.

steps.text: 어때요? means 'how is it?'. Use it for weather, food, anything.
비가 와요 means 'it's raining', literally 'rain comes'.

steps.why: 비가 와요: rain comes.
어때요? asks how something is.

steps.text: 잘했어요! You can talk about the weather now.
Let's review everything from Units 1 to 5. No new grammar, just practice.

steps.why: 저 ends in a vowel, so 는.
의사 ends in a vowel, so 가 아니에요.
빵 ends in a consonant, so 을.
의 shows who owns it: a friend's bag.
The vowel is ㅗ, so 아요.
Stem 춥 + 지 않아요.
Vowel stem, so ㅂ니다.

steps.translation: My older sister is a nurse.
I drink coffee with a friend.

steps.text: 대단해요! You finished the first five units. Gochi is proud of you.
Let's learn words for friends, gifts and messages.

steps.why: 선물 is a gift. 편지 is a letter.
보내다 is to send. 주다 is to give.
축하해요 means congratulations.

steps.text: 에게 and 한테 mean 'to' a person. 한테 is more casual. Both work after any name.

steps.translation: I send a letter to a friend.

steps.text: Some verbs shorten in the 요 style. 주다 becomes 줘요, 보다 becomes 봐요, 마시다 becomes 마셔요.

steps.translation: I give flowers to my mother.

steps.text: For places, use 에, not 에게. 에게 is only for people and animals.

steps.why: 에게 means 'to' a person.
한테 is common in speech. 에게 is more written.
주 + 어요 shortens to 줘요.

steps.translation: I give a gift to my older sister.

steps.text: 만 means 'only'. Put it right after the noun.

steps.translation: Only my younger sibling is coming.

steps.text: Like 도, 만 replaces 을/를 and 이/가.
I only eat bread: 빵___ 먹어요.
steps.why: 만 means only. 도 means too.
만 replaces 을/를.
만 means only.

steps.translation: This is a gift for you.
Wow, thank you! Is it flowers?
Yes. And there's a letter too.

steps.why: 고마워요 is a friendly thank you.
한테 means 'to' a person.

steps.translation: I send a letter to my friend.

steps.text: 잘했어요! You can give gifts and send messages now.

units.title: Where things are
units.subtitle: Say where things are and where you do things

steps.text: Let's learn words to say where things are.

steps.translation: to not be there, to not have

steps.why: 옆 means next to. 뒤 means behind.

steps.text: Which is the opposite of 있다?
steps.why: 있다 is 'there is', 없다 is 'there isn't'.
침대 is a bed.

steps.text: To say where something is, use place + 에 + 있어요.

steps.translation: The cat is in the room.

steps.text: For positions, say the thing first, then the position word, then 에.

steps.translation: The book is on the desk.
The bag is under the chair.

steps.text: To ask where, use 어디에 있어요?

steps.why: Where something is: 에 있어요.

steps.text: How do you say 'next to the desk'?
steps.why: Thing first, then 옆, then 에.
없어요 means there isn't.

steps.translation: The cat is under the bed.

steps.text: 에서 marks the place where an action happens.
Compare: 에 is for being somewhere. 에서 is for doing something there.

steps.why: 배우다 is an action, so 에서.
있다 is being somewhere, so 에.
Watching is an action, so 에서.

lessons.title: Put it together: where are you?

steps.translation: I'm home. I'm watching a drama in my room.

steps.ko: 제 가방이 하나 씨 집에 있어요?
steps.translation: Is my bag at your place?
Yes, it's next to the chair.

steps.text: 지금 means now. 내일 means tomorrow.

steps.why: Being somewhere: 에.
어디 means where.

steps.text: 잘했어요! You can say where things are now.

units.title: Dates
units.subtitle: Talk about days and the past

steps.text: Korean has two number systems. This one, from Chinese, is for dates, money and phone numbers.
Months are number + 월. Watch out: June is 유월 and October is 시월.

steps.why: June is 유월, not 육월.
토요일 is Saturday. 일요일 is Sunday.

steps.text: The past works like -아요/어요. Just use 았어요 or 었어요 instead.
If the last vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ, use 았어요.
Other vowels, use 었어요. 하다 becomes 했어요.

steps.why: The vowel in 먹 is ㅓ, so 었어요.
하다 becomes 했어요.
The vowel in 작 is ㅏ, so 았어요.

steps.text: To say when something happens, add 에 after the time.

steps.translation: I met a friend on Saturday.
I'm going to Korea in March.
What did you do on the weekend?

steps.text: 어제, 오늘 and 내일 don't take 에.

steps.why: Time + 에.
어제 never takes 에.
했어요 is the past of 해요.

steps.translation: I met a friend on the weekend.
What did you do on the weekend?

steps.ko: 토요일에 친구를 만났어요. 같이 영화를 봤어요.
steps.translation: I met a friend on Saturday. We watched a movie together.
It was really good! On Sunday I rested at home.

steps.text: 어땠어요? is the past of 어때요?. 같이 means together.
쉬다 means to rest. 쉬었어요 is its past.

steps.why: 어땠어요 is past.
Time + 에.

steps.text: 잘했어요! You can talk about the past now.

units.title: Sports
units.subtitle: Say what you can and can't do

steps.text: Let's learn sports and words for how often.

steps.why: 축구 is soccer. 야구 is baseball.
가끔 is sometimes. 자주 is often.
잘 means well: 잘해요, I'm good at it.

steps.text: 부터 means 'from' and 까지 means 'until'. Use them with times and days.

steps.translation: I work from Monday to Friday.

steps.why: 부터 means from or starting.
까지 means until.
부터 comes first, then 까지.

steps.translation: I swim from Monday to Friday.

steps.text: 못 means 'can't'. Put it right before the verb.
You can also add 지 못해요 to the stem. It means the same, a bit more formal.
Compare: 안 (short for -지 않아요) means you don't. 못 means you can't.
I can't drink coffee: 커피를 ___ 마셔요.
steps.why: 못 + verb means can't.
Stem 가 + 지 못해요.
못 means can't. 안 means don't.

steps.text: Hana and Minsu talk about sports. Listen.

steps.translation: I like soccer. I play every day.

steps.ko: 저는 수영을 잘해요. 월요일부터 금요일까지 수영장에 가요.
steps.translation: I'm good at swimming. I go to the pool Monday to Friday.

steps.text: 무슨 means 'what kind of'. 수영장 is a swimming pool.

steps.why: 잘 + 해요 means you do it well.
못 means can't.

steps.text: 잘했어요! You can talk about sports now.
This is the native Korean number system. Use it for counting things and for hours.
Before 시 (o'clock), some shorten: 한 시, 두 시, 세 시, 네 시.
Minutes use the other system: 삼십 분 is 30 minutes.

steps.why: 넷 shortens to 네 before 시.
다섯 is 5.
Hours use native numbers, minutes use 일, 이, 삼.

steps.text: -을까요? means 'shall we?'. Use it to suggest something.
After a consonant add 을까요. After a vowel add ㄹ까요.
-읍시다 means 'let's'. After a vowel it's ㅂ시다.
-읍시다 can sound bossy to older people. With them, use -을까요? instead.

steps.why: Vowel stem, so ㄹ까요: 마실까요.
Consonant stem, so 을까요.
Vowel stem, so ㅂ시다.

steps.text: -고 joins two actions or descriptions, like 'and'. Add it to the stem.

steps.translation: I eat and (then) watch a movie.
The weather is nice and warm.
I did my homework and slept.

steps.text: The tense goes on the last verb only.
I ate and drank. Which is right?
steps.why: Past goes on the last verb: 먹고 마셨어요.
Stem 공부하 + 고.
-고 means and.

steps.translation: I'll eat lunch and drink coffee.

steps.text: Minsu asks Hana to lunch. Listen.

steps.ko: 하나 씨, 내일 같이 점심을 먹을까요?
steps.translation: Hana, shall we have lunch tomorrow?
Sure! What time shall we meet?
Shall we have lunch and then coffee too?
Yes, sounds good. See you tomorrow!

steps.text: 몇 시 means 'what time'. 내일 봐요 means 'see you tomorrow'.

steps.why: 몇 means how many: 몇 시 is what time.
Vowel stem, so ㅂ시다.

steps.translation: Shall we watch a movie together?

steps.text: 잘했어요! You can make plans in Korean now.

steps.why: 한테 means 'to' a person.
만 means only.
Being somewhere: 에.
An action somewhere: 에서.
보 + 았어요 shortens to 봤어요.
부터 ... 까지: from ... to.
못 means can't.
Consonant stem, so 을까요.

steps.translation: I met a friend on Saturday.
Shall we eat and then watch a movie?

steps.text: 대단해요! You finished ten units. Gochi is very proud.
